mainEntity.name: What is the difference between the binomial and hypergeometric distributions?

acceptedAnswer.text: The binomial model assumes independent trials with a constant probability, as with sampling with replacement or from a very large population. The hypergeometric distribution models sampling without replacement from a finite population, where each draw changes the odds of the next. When the sample is a small fraction of the population (commonly under 5%), the binomial is a good approximation.

mainEntity.name: When can I use a normal approximation?

acceptedAnswer.text: A common rule of thumb is that both np and n(1 − p) should be at least 5 (some texts use 10). Then X is approximately normal with mean np and standard deviation √(npq), usually with a continuity correction of ±0.5. This calculator gives the exact answer, so no approximation is needed.

mainEntity.name: How does the calculator avoid overflow for large n?

acceptedAnswer.text: Instead of multiplying huge factorials, it works with the logarithm of the binomial coefficient (using the log-gamma function) and exponentiates at the end. The exact coefficient shown in the steps is computed separately with integer arithmetic.

mainEntity.name: What happens when p is 0 or 1?

acceptedAnswer.text: The outcome is certain: if p = 0 every trial fails, so P(X = 0) = 1; if p = 1 every trial succeeds, so P(X = n) = 1. The variance is zero and the distribution is a single point.

mainEntity.name: How do I find the probability of at least one success?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use the complement: P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(X = 0) = 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ. Set k = 1 and choose P(X ≥ k) to see it directly.

mainEntity.name: What if my trials are not independent?

acceptedAnswer.text: Then the binomial model does not apply exactly. Depending on the situation, a hypergeometric or other model may be more suitable. Independence and a constant probability are essential assumptions.

mainEntity.name: How do I find the probability between two values, P(a ≤ X ≤ b)?

acceptedAnswer.text: Subtract two cumulative results: P(X ≤ b) − P(X ≤ a − 1). For n = 10, p = 0.5 and 4 to 6 successes that is 0.828125 − 0.171875 = 0.65625.

mainEntity.name: What are binompdf and binomcdf, and how do they match this calculator?

acceptedAnswer.text: On a TI-83 or TI-84, binompdf(n, p, k) is the exact probability P(X = k) and binomcdf(n, p, k) is the cumulative probability P(X ≤ k). Enter the same n, p and k here and read P(X = k) and P(X ≤ k).

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate a binomial probability in Excel or Google Sheets?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use =BINOM.DIST(k, n, p, FALSE) for the exact probability and =BINOM.DIST(k, n, p, TRUE) for the cumulative probability. For n = 10, p = 0.5, k = 3 they return 0.117188 and 0.171875.

mainEntity.name: When should I use the Poisson approximation instead of the normal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use Poisson when n is large and p is small, with λ = np. For n = 50 and p = 0.02, the exact P(X ≤ 2) is 0.921572 and the Poisson value with λ = 1 is 0.919699. The normal approximation works better when p is near 0.5.

mainEntity.name: Can the variance of a binomial distribution be larger than its mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The variance npq is never more than the mean np, because q is at most 1. They are nearly equal when p is very small, and the variance is largest relative to n when p = 0.5.
